summary: Specifies how IRC servers manage channels, including their characteristics and properties. It covers the rules that govern how groups of users meet in a named conversation space. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2811 describes how Internet Relay Chat (IRC) servers manage channels, including who may join, speak or change settings. It also explains how channel names and state are handled when servers split and reconnect.

subtitle: How IRC servers name channels, manage membership and apply channel modes.

tldr.problem: IRC channels can have different scopes, lifetimes and access rules, so servers need shared rules for managing them and handling network splits.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines four channel-name prefixes, channel operators and creators, channel modes, access masks and rules for ordinary and safe channels.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2811 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1459. It also describes known problems with collisions, privacy and access control.

today: RFC 2811 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1459. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes RFC 2811.

sections.title: What a Channel Is
sections.content:
An IRC channel is a named group of users who receive messages sent to the channel. It has a name, properties and current members. This memo describes how IRC servers manage channels and is aimed mainly at server implementers.

The document builds on the IRC architecture and defines channel concepts and modes. The channel rules are important for servers, while simple clients can be implemented without the full details.
sections.plainLanguage: A channel groups users who want to receive the same messages. IRC servers use these rules to manage the channel and its members.

sections.title: Channel Names and Scope
sections.content:
Channel names are case-insensitive strings of up to fifty characters. They begin with &, number sign, + or !, and must not contain spaces, control-G or commas. The prefixes create separate name spaces.

A channel is known to one or more servers, and those servers must form a contiguous part of the IRC network so they can deliver channel messages. Names beginning with & identify channels local to one server. Other channels may be known across the network or limited by a channel mask.
sections.plainLanguage: The first character of a channel name identifies its channel type. Some channels exist on one server; others are shared by servers that know about them.

sections.title: Operators and Channel Lifetime
sections.content:
Channel operators can invite or remove users, change modes and manage the topic when the topic is restricted. Operators share ownership of a channel. On a channel whose name begins with !, the user who creates it also receives channel-creator status, which permits changes that operators cannot make.

Standard channels beginning with &, number sign or + are created when the first user joins and end when the last user leaves. The memo describes Channel Delay to reduce duplicate names after a network split. A channel name may be temporarily unavailable to local users after an operator leaves because of a split.
sections.plainLanguage: Channel operators can change channel settings and manage members. Standard channels exist while they have members, while a delay can prevent an immediate reuse of a name after a network split.

sections.title: Channel Modes and Access Control
sections.content:
Modes control member status, channel properties and access. The member modes include operator status and voice, which lets a member speak in a moderated channel. Channel flags include invite-only, moderated, no outside messages, private, secret and topic restrictions. A channel key and user limit can also be set.

Ban masks can prevent a matching user from joining; exception masks can override a ban, and invitation masks can allow joining an invite-only channel. Private and secret channels hide their existence from some queries. The two flags must not both be set at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: Channel modes control who can join, speak, invite people or change settings. Access masks can block a user, make an exception or allow a matching user into an invite-only channel.

sections.title: Known Problems and Security
sections.content:
When servers reconnect, channel members from both sides may be combined. This can expose membership or let users gain operator status through a channel collision. Servers may also disagree temporarily about channel modes, and conflicting key or user-limit values have no defined winner.

Address-based access masks depend on accurate user and host information, which the RFC says many public networks do not provide. A channel key is sent in plaintext and can be exposed to a man-in-the-middle attack. The anonymous flag masks message origins between server and client but does not provide anonymity between servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Channel access rules have limits when servers reconnect or when user identity information is unreliable. The RFC warns that plaintext channel keys can be intercepted and that its anonymous mode does not hide users from servers.
